title: When to Fine-Tune & Data
scopeHtml: Scope: Prompting vs RAG vs fine-tuning, data collection and quality.

notes.title: Prompting vs RAG vs fine-tuning
notes.html:
What each lever changes.

Lever What changes Persistence Cost to change
Prompting instructions and examples at inference time per request seconds, free
RAG which external facts are available index content minutes, cheap
Fine-tuning the model's weights (behaviour, style, skills) permanent until retrained hours/days, data + compute + eval
Tools access to live data and actions integration engineering

Decision framework. Ask what is wrong:

  1. The model doesn't know the facts (private, new, changing) → RAG (or tools for live data). Fine-tuning is a poor and costly way to inject facts: it's unreliable at memorizing, hard to update, and gives no citations.
  2. The model knows but doesn't behave the way I need (format, tone, domain conventions, consistent style, reliable tool use) → prompting first; if prompts get long/fragile or small-model cost/latency matters → fine-tuning.
  3. Needs both → fine-tune for behaviour, RAG for knowledge.
  4. Latency/cost at scale → fine-tune a smaller model (distillation) to replace long prompts and large models.
  5. Needs actions/real-time data → tools.

Order of attack. Better prompt + examples → add retrieval → add tools → fine-tune → (rarely) continued pretraining. Each step should be justified by an eval gap.

Real life. Briefing a chef (prompt), handing them a recipe book (RAG), sending them to culinary school (fine-tuning), giving them a phone to call the supplier (tools).

Interview angle. The classic: "Should we fine-tune to teach the model our documentation?" Answer: RAG for facts; fine-tune only for behaviour.

notes.title: When fine-tuning is worth it
notes.html:
Good reasons.

  • Consistent format or voice that prompts can't hold reliably (strict JSON dialects, brand tone, clinical note style).
  • Narrow, high-volume task where a small tuned model matches a large prompted model at 10 to 100x lower cost and latency.
  • Removing long prompts/few-shot examples (they cost tokens on every call) by baking behaviour into weights.
  • Domain skills with specialized vocabulary or conventions (legal clauses, medical coding, internal DSLs, code style).
  • Improved tool-calling reliability for your specific API surface.
  • Distillation from a stronger model into a cheaper one.
  • On-device/offline or privacy-constrained deployments with open-weight models.
  • Behaviour alignment (refusal policy, safety style) with preference tuning.

Bad reasons. "Teach it our docs" (use RAG); fixing hallucinations about changing facts; compensating for no eval; avoiding prompt engineering effort; expecting to fix reasoning capability limits of a small model.

Checklist before starting.

  1. A baseline: best-effort prompting (with examples) on the target model and a stronger one.
  2. A measurable eval and a target (e.g. ≥ 95% format-valid, ≥ X accuracy, cost ≤ Y).
  3. Enough quality data (see below) or a plan to produce it.
  4. Maintenance plan: retraining when requirements change; versioning.
  5. Cost-benefit: training + hosting vs prompt tokens saved.

Real life. Train a specialist when the job is repeated thousands of times; don't send someone to school for a one-off errand.

notes.title: Data: the main determinant of quality
notes.html:
Quantity vs quality. For instruction/behaviour tuning, a few hundred to a few thousand high-quality, diverse examples often beat tens of thousands of noisy ones (the "less is more" finding). Larger sets help for complex skills or new domains.

Sourcing.

  • Production logs (best distribution match) filtered for good outcomes and cleaned/anonymized.
  • Expert demonstrations written or corrected by domain experts.
  • Synthetic data generated by a stronger model from seed tasks, then filtered with validators/judges/execution checks and diversified; always include real data in the mix.
  • Public datasets (check licences).
  • Corrections collected from user edits and human review (high value: they target real errors).

Quality criteria. Correct; consistent style and format; matches the exact prompt format and chat template used at inference; diverse in topics, lengths, difficulty; includes edge cases, refusals, "unknown", and tool-error recovery; de-duplicated; free of PII/secrets and licence-restricted content; balanced across classes/categories.

Splits and leakage. Train/validation/test split by group (not random rows) so near-duplicates or the same customer don't leak across splits; hold out a test set that is never used for tuning.

Annotation process. Clear guidelines with examples; calibration rounds; measure inter-annotator agreement; audit samples; track label noise; iterate on guidelines.

Real life. Teaching by good worked examples, not by volume of homework.

notes.title: Data formats and pitfalls
notes.html:
Formats.

  • Instruction/SFT: {"messages": [{"role":"system"},{"role":"user"},{"role":"assistant"}]}; loss on assistant tokens only; multi-turn supported; include tool calls and tool results in the same schema used at inference.
  • Completion format for base models.
  • Preference data (DPO): {prompt, chosen, rejected}.
  • Classification/regression heads or labels as text.
  • Reasoning traces (chain-of-thought) for distillation of reasoning.

Pitfalls.

  • Template mismatch between training and inference (silent quality loss).
  • Label noise and inconsistent style (the model averages them).
  • Contamination of the eval set with training data.
  • Training on model outputs where the provider's terms prohibit it.
  • PII and secrets memorized and regurgitated.
  • Overly narrow data causing catastrophic forgetting of general abilities.
  • Over-represented patterns (the model learns shortcuts, e.g. always answering "yes").
  • Truncation: training examples exceeding max length cut mid-answer.
  • Class imbalance and missing negative/edge examples.
  • Distribution shift between curated data and real traffic.

Real life. Garbage in the textbook, garbage in the student.

notes.title: Build the eval first
notes.html:
Process.

  1. Define target behaviours and metrics (accuracy/F1, format validity, rubric score, latency, cost, safety).
  2. Build a held-out test set that reflects production, including hard and adversarial cases and general-capability probes (to detect forgetting).
  3. Baseline: evaluate the base model with the best prompt; evaluate a stronger model as an upper reference.
  4. Fine-tune; evaluate on the same set with the same grader; compare with confidence intervals.
  5. Check regressions: general benchmarks, safety/refusal behaviour, other tasks.
  6. Evaluate cost/latency/serving requirements.
  7. Decide: ship, iterate on data/hyperparameters, or abandon if the gain doesn't justify the cost.

If you cannot measure improvement, do not fine-tune.

Real life. Take a "before" photo so you can tell whether the diet worked.

notes.title: Summary
notes.html:
Choosing the lever. Prompting for quick behaviour/format control; RAG for knowledge (private, fresh, large, with citations); tools for live data/actions; fine-tuning for stable behaviour, style, narrow high-volume tasks, lower cost/latency, shorter prompts, distillation. Fine-tuning is a poor way to add facts.

Worth it when. Prompts can't hold format/voice; a small tuned model can replace a large prompted one; long few-shot prompts are costly; domain conventions or tool reliability need to improve. Prerequisites: baseline, eval, data, maintenance plan.

Data. Quality and diversity beat volume; use real logs, expert demonstrations, filtered synthetic data and corrections; match the inference template exactly; include edge cases and refusals; de-duplicate; split by group; watch PII and licences.

Pitfalls. Template mismatch, label noise, contamination, forgetting, shortcuts, truncation, distribution shift, terms-of-use violations.

Evaluate first. Held-out test set, baselines (prompted base and stronger model), regression checks, cost/latency; no measurable gain means no fine-tune.

Interview one-liners.

  • "RAG is for knowledge, fine-tuning is for behaviour."
  • "Data quality is the model."
  • "Train on exactly the format you will serve."
  • "No eval, no fine-tune."

questions.promptHtml: Our LLM feature gives wrong answers. How do you decide whether the fix is prompting, RAG, or fine-tuning?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: The first question in every GenAI project. It shows whether you diagnose the failure type before reaching for the most expensive tool.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: I ask what is actually wrong. If the model lacks facts (private, new, or changing information), I use RAG, which means fetching relevant documents at request time and pasting them into the prompt. If the model knows enough but behaves wrongly (format, tone, conventions), I try prompting first, and fine-tune (continue training the model's weights on my own examples) only if prompts stay fragile, long, or too costly. If it needs live data or actions, I add tools. Facts go in context; behaviour goes in weights.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Terms first. A prompt is the text you send the model: instructions plus examples. RAG (retrieval-augmented generation) searches your documents and adds the best passages to the prompt. Fine-tuning changes the model's weights using example input/output pairs. Tools let the model call your APIs.

Symptom                                   -> Lever
Doesn't know our policy / old data        -> RAG (or tools for live data)
Knows, but wrong format/tone              -> Prompt + examples -> fine-tune if it stays flaky
Prompt is 3k tokens of rules, too costly  -> Fine-tune (smaller model)
Needs today's price / to create a ticket  -> Tools
Both behaviour and knowledge              -> Fine-tune for behaviour + RAG for knowledge

Each lever changes something different: prompting changes instructions per request (seconds, free); RAG changes which facts are visible (minutes, cheap); fine-tuning changes weights permanently until retrained (hours or days, plus data, compute, and evaluation); tools change what the model can reach. The cost of changing your mind rises down that list, so you start at the top and move down only when an evaluation shows a gap.

Diagnosis in practice: take 50 to 100 real failures and label each as "missing fact", "wrong behaviour", "needs live data", or "reasoning too weak". The label counts tell you the lever. Reasoning-too-weak is none of these: it usually means a bigger model, not fine-tuning a small one.

sections.label: Code
sections.html: Not applicable: this is a decision framework. See the data-format and evaluation questions for code.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Jumping to fine-tuning because it feels like "real" AI work.
  • Treating every wrong answer as one problem instead of labelling failures first.
  • Fine-tuning to fix hallucinations about facts that change weekly.
  • Skipping the baseline: no best-effort prompt result to compare against.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. When do you combine them? → Fine-tune for output style and tool use, RAG for the knowledge it should cite.
  2. What if the failure is bad reasoning? → Try a stronger model or better decomposition; a small tuned model will not gain reasoning it never had.
  3. How do you show the lever choice was right? → An eval before and after, with the gap closed per failure category.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3 YOE: "RAG for knowledge, fine-tune for style." Senior: labels real failures first, orders levers by cost of change, justifies each step with an eval gap, and combines levers where both failure types exist.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A team spent a month fine-tuning on product manuals; most remaining failures were stale prices that a single tool call would have fixed.

questions.promptHtml: In what order would you try improvements on an LLM feature, and why is fine-tuning usually late in that order?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Checks cost awareness and engineering discipline. Candidates who say "fine-tune first" tend to over-spend.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Better prompt with examples first, then retrieval, then tools, then fine-tuning, and continued pretraining (training on a large raw corpus before instruction tuning) almost never. The order follows cost and reversibility: a prompt edit takes seconds and is free to undo, while fine-tuning needs data, compute, an eval, and retraining whenever requirements change. Each step must be justified by a measured gap on an evaluation set.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Think of it as a ladder where each rung costs more and locks you in more.

Step Typical cost Reversible? Moves when
Prompt + few-shot examples minutes instantly always first
Retrieval (RAG) days to build index yes, re-index facts missing
Tools engineering weeks yes live data/actions
Fine-tuning data + GPU + eval + hosting retrain needed behaviour gap persists, or cost/latency pressure
Continued pretraining very large corpus + compute no new language/domain at scale, rare

Why fine-tuning is late: (1) you need labelled data you may not have, (2) it can cause catastrophic forgetting (the model loses general skills while learning the narrow one), (3) every change in requirements means a new training run, (4) with provider-hosted models, new base-model releases may leave your tuned model outdated.

"Justified by an eval gap" means: before moving down the ladder, show that the previous rung's best version still misses your target (for example 88% valid JSON vs a 98% target).

sections.label: Code
sections.html: Not applicable: process question.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Counting "tried prompting" after one lazy prompt rather than a serious attempt with examples.
  • Adding RAG when the failure is formatting.
  • Ignoring that a stronger prompted model may beat a tuned weaker one.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. When might you skip rungs? → Strict privacy or on-device constraints can force a small open-weight model, where fine-tuning is the first lever.
  2. How many prompt attempts count as a fair baseline? → Enough to include clear instructions, 3 to 10 curated examples, and a stronger-model reference.
  3. Does fine-tuning ever replace RAG? → Rarely; it does not update easily or cite sources.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3 YOE recites the order. Senior ties each step to an eval gap and a maintenance cost, and names the lock-in each step creates.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: One team fine-tuned in week one, then a spec change in week five made the dataset obsolete; a prompt edit would have absorbed it in minutes.

questions.promptHtml: What does a supervised fine-tuning (SFT) example look like, and which tokens does the model actually learn from?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Tests whether you have touched real training data. Many failures start in the data format.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: SFT (supervised fine-tuning) means training on input/output pairs. In the common chat format, each example is a list of messages with roles (system, user, assistant). The loss, the number that training minimises, is computed only on the assistant tokens; the system and user tokens are given as context but masked out. Multi-turn chats and tool calls use the same schema as at inference time.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
One JSON object per line (JSONL):

{"messages":[
  {"role":"system","content":"You extract invoices as JSON."},
  {"role":"user","content":"Invoice #81 total 40 EUR"},
  {"role":"assistant","content":"{\"id\":81,\"total\":40,\"cur\":\"EUR\"}"}
]}

Training flow: the messages are rendered through the model's chat template (the exact text layout with special tokens that marks roles) into one token sequence. A loss mask marks which tokens count. The model predicts each next token; the error is only counted where the mask is 1 (the assistant's reply). Why: you want it to learn to write answers, not to imitate user questions.

Other formats: plain completion text for base models; preference triples {prompt, chosen, rejected} for DPO (direct preference optimisation, which teaches the model to prefer one answer over another); reasoning traces for distilling step-by-step thinking.

Tool use: include assistant tool-call messages and tool results in the same structure you use in production, otherwise the model never sees what a call really looks like.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
import json
example = {"messages": [
    {"role": "system", "content": "You extract invoices as JSON."},
    {"role": "user", "content": "Invoice #81 total 40 EUR"},
    {"role": "assistant", "content": '{"id":81,"total":40,"cur":"EUR"}'},
]}
with open("train.jsonl", "a", encoding="utf-8") as f:
    f.write(json.dumps(example) + "\n")   # one example per line
// Uses kotlinx.serialization or Jackson in practice; plain map shown for clarity
val example = mapOf("messages" to listOf(
    mapOf("role" to "system", "content" to "You extract invoices as JSON."),
    mapOf("role" to "user", "content" to "Invoice #81 total 40 EUR"),
    mapOf("role" to "assistant", "content" to """{"id":81,"total":40,"cur":"EUR"}"""),
))
// serialize with your JSON library, append one line per example to train.jsonl
// Jackson: new ObjectMapper().writeValueAsString(example) then append + "\n"
var example = java.util.Map.of("messages", java.util.List.of(
    java.util.Map.of("role", "system", "content", "You extract invoices as JSON."),
    java.util.Map.of("role", "user", "content", "Invoice #81 total 40 EUR"),
    java.util.Map.of("role", "assistant", "content", "{\"id\":81,\"total\":40,\"cur\":\"EUR\"}")));

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Writing pretty-printed multi-line JSON instead of one object per line.
  • Training on the user tokens too (when the framework lets you), which teaches the model to write user text.
  • Omitting the system prompt that production will send.
  • Different role names or tool schema than inference.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. What is a chat template? → The model-specific string layout with special tokens marking roles and turns.
  2. What is DPO data? → Prompt plus a chosen and a rejected answer.
  3. How do you train tool use? → Include tool-call and tool-result messages exactly as the serving stack produces them.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3 YOE shows the JSON. Senior explains loss masking and the template, and knows both must match serving.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A job trained with loss on all tokens made the model sometimes continue the user's message instead of answering.

questions.promptHtml: A stakeholder says "just fine-tune the model on our wiki so it knows our product." Why is that usually the wrong tool?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: The classic trap question. The answer reveals whether you understand what weights are good at.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Fine-tuning shapes behaviour well but stores facts poorly. The model may only partly memorise the wiki, it can blend or invent details with confidence, it cannot cite where an answer came from, and every wiki change means retraining. RAG keeps facts in an index you can update in minutes, with citations. I would use RAG for the knowledge and fine-tune only if the style or format needs it.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
During training the model adjusts billions of numbers so that it predicts text better. Facts get spread across those numbers in a lossy way; rare facts (a single policy sentence) are exactly the ones that are least reliably retained. The result is plausible-sounding answers that mix details, a hallucination (a confident wrong statement).

Concrete contrasts:

  • Freshness: a policy changes Monday. RAG: re-index the page. Fine-tune: new dataset, training run, evaluation, redeploy.
  • Citations and access control: RAG can show the source and filter by user permission. Weights cannot; whatever was trained in can be asked out by anyone.
  • Deletion: removing one document from an index is trivial; removing it from weights is not.
  • Cost: index storage vs repeated training.

When fine-tuning on docs still helps: the model needs the company's vocabulary and phrasing (for example internal acronyms) or a fixed answer style. That is behaviour, and it is learned from question/answer examples, not by dumping raw text.

sections.label: Code
sections.html: Not applicable: conceptual comparison.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Believing more training epochs equals better memory of facts.
  • Forgetting access control: private data inside weights is available to all users.
  • Calling a fine-tuned model "up to date" after a doc change.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. What if retrieval quality is poor? → Fix chunking, search, and reranking; that is still cheaper than weights.
  2. Could you do both? → Yes: tune for citation style and abstaining, retrieve for the facts.
  3. How would you measure knowledge-injection success? → Held-out questions whose answers appear only in the new documents, versus a RAG baseline.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3 YOE: "RAG is for knowledge." Senior adds freshness, citation, permissions, deletion, and lossy storage as concrete reasons, and keeps a role for tuning on behaviour.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A tuned model kept quoting a discontinued refund window for months after the policy changed.

questions.promptHtml: Give the legitimate reasons to fine-tune, and explain how a small tuned model can replace a large prompted one.

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Tests whether you can name real value drivers (cost, latency, consistency) rather than vague "better quality".

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Good reasons are: a consistent format or voice that prompts cannot hold, a narrow high-volume task where a small tuned model matches a large prompted one at far lower cost and latency, removing long few-shot prompts that cost tokens on every call, domain conventions (legal, medical coding, internal languages), more reliable tool calling for my API, distillation from a stronger model, and on-device or privacy-bound deployments. Bad reasons are teaching docs, fixing changing facts, or avoiding prompt work.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Distillation means using a strong, expensive model (the teacher) to generate or label examples, then training a small cheap model (the student) on them so it copies the teacher on one narrow task. It works because a narrow task needs far fewer capabilities than a general chat model has.

Why it can be cheaper: a hosted large model charges per token and spends tokens on a long instruction prompt every call. A tuned small model has the instructions "baked in", so the prompt can be 50 tokens instead of 2,000, and the model itself is smaller and faster.

Large model + 2,000-token prompt   : high $/call, ~1.5 s
Small tuned model + 50-token prompt: much lower $/call, ~0.3 s   (numbers illustrative; measure yours)

What it cannot do: add reasoning ability beyond the student's size, or inject changing facts. Tuned models also need retraining when the task spec changes, so the saving must exceed training, hosting, and maintenance cost.

Other legitimate drivers: strict JSON dialects where one malformed output breaks a downstream parser; alignment of refusal style through preference tuning; an offline mobile or edge model that must run without a network.

sections.label: Code
sections.html: Not applicable: reasoning question. See the break-even scenario for the calculation.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Claiming "higher quality" without a baseline against the strongest prompted model.
  • Ignoring hosting cost for a self-served tuned model.
  • Expecting the student to beat the teacher on tasks outside the training distribution.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. What is the main risk of distillation? → The student inherits teacher errors, and terms of service may restrict using outputs for training.
  2. Does fine-tuning reduce latency? → Often yes via a smaller model and shorter prompt; verify by measuring.
  3. When is a long prompt better? → When requirements change weekly.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3 YOE lists benefits. Senior frames each as a measurable target (cost per call, format validity) and checks maintenance and terms of use.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A classification task running at 3 million calls a day moved from a large prompted model to a tuned small one and cut the inference bill sharply with equal accuracy on the eval set.

questions.contextHtml: A product manager at a 400-person insurer asks you to "fine-tune a model on our 6,000 policy PDFs so the support bot stops getting things wrong." Current state: a prompted hosted model with no retrieval. A sample of 100 failed conversations from last month shows: 58 wrong or outdated policy details, 17 answers in the wrong tone for regulated communications, 12 where the bot needed the customer's live claim status, and 13 reasoning slips on multi-step premium calculations. Policies are revised about every two weeks. The budget is one engineer for six weeks.
questions.promptHtml: What do you propose, and how do you handle the request as stated?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Sure, fine-tune on the PDFs." That ignores that 58% of failures are facts that change every two weeks, that permissions and citations matter in insurance, and that no baseline or eval exists.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Are answers legally binding, so do they need citations? Who may see which policies (permission filters)? Can I get the 100 failures plus a gold set of 200 questions with correct answers? Is there a tone guide? Which model is the baseline and can I use a stronger one as a reference?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Add a "verify with an agent" fallback and block premium calculations from free-text answers until fixed.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: 58 facts failures: RAG. 12 live status: a claims-status tool. 17 tone: system prompt plus examples, fine-tuning later if still flaky. 13 reasoning slips: move calculations into a deterministic tool or a stronger model.
  4. How I'd verify each: Label the 100 failures by hand (second reviewer on 20 for agreement), build the 200-question gold set, run the current prompt as baseline, then measure each lever's gain separately.
  5. Root cause: The bot has no access to current policy text and is being asked to remember it.
  6. Fix: Week 1-2 RAG with chunking by policy section and citations; week 3 claims tool; week 4 tone prompt with 5 examples and a calculation tool; week 5-6 evaluate and decide if tone tuning is justified.
  7. Prevention: Re-index on every policy revision; regression eval in CI; logging of retrieved passage IDs.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not train on the PDFs: revisions every two weeks would make the weights stale, there would be no citations, and policy content would be extractable by any user. I would explain this to the PM with the failure counts.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• The PM insists on fine-tuning for "ownership of the model" → Offer tuning for tone and abstaining behaviour on top of RAG, using conversation examples, not PDFs.
  • Retrieval recall is only 70% → Improve chunking, hybrid search, and reranking, and measure recall at k on the gold set before touching weights.
  • Legal says no data may leave the country → Self-host an open-weight model; fine-tuning may become the first lever then.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite team trained on a policy corpus, shipped, and a week later a revision made the bot confidently quote the old rule. The fix was a retrieval layer, which they should have built first.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: agrees to fine-tune on the PDFs.
  • Hire: proposes RAG for facts, tool for status, and prompt for tone, with a baseline.
  • Strong hire: also labels failures, builds the gold set, adds permissions and citations, and keeps tuning as a measured later option.

questions.promptHtml: What must be in place before you start a fine-tuning project?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Separates people who have shipped from people who have only trained in a notebook.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Five things. A baseline: the best-effort prompt, with examples, on both the target model and a stronger one. A measurable eval with a target number. Enough quality data, or a plan to make it. A maintenance plan for retraining and versioning. A cost-benefit comparison of training plus hosting against the prompt tokens or larger model it replaces. If any is missing, I fix that first.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
1. Baseline. Without it you cannot say the tuned model is better. The stronger-model result is the ceiling you are trying to approach cheaply.
  2. Eval and target. For example: at least 95% valid JSON, at least X% field accuracy, p95 latency under 400 ms, cost under Y per 1,000 calls. A target turns "better" into a stop condition.
  3. Data. Quality and diversity matter more than volume (see the data questions). Plan sourcing, cleaning, PII removal, and licences.
  4. Maintenance. When requirements change, who regenerates data, retrains, re-evaluates, and rolls out? Version datasets and models together.
  5. Cost-benefit. Training compute, labelling hours, hosting a model (or tuned-model surcharge at a provider), versus prompt tokens saved.

Break-even sketch: if the tuned model saves $S per 1,000 calls and the project costs $P, you need 1,000 × P / S calls to recoup it. Include engineer time in P; teams often forget it.

sections.label: Code
sections.html: Not applicable: checklist question.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Starting with data collection before defining the metric.
  • Comparing the tuned model with a weak prompt instead of the best prompt.
  • Forgetting that the base model gets deprecated and the tuned one must be redone.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. What if you have no data? → Start with prompts and log outputs plus human edits to build it.
  2. How do you set the target? → From the business need and the stronger-model ceiling.
  3. What if the project fails the cost-benefit? → Stay on prompting; document why.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3 YOE: "need a dataset." Senior lists baseline, target, maintenance, and break-even, and treats "abandon" as an acceptable outcome.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A tuned model hit its accuracy goal but cost more to host than the prompt tokens it saved at the actual traffic volume.

questions.promptHtml: For instruction or behaviour fine-tuning, is more data better? What matters most in a dataset?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Tests your mental model of what the model learns from, and whether you will waste money on volume.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Not always. For behaviour tuning, a few hundred to a few thousand high-quality, diverse, consistent examples often beat tens of thousands of noisy ones. What matters most is correctness, consistent format and style, a match to the exact prompt format used in production, diversity of topics, lengths, and difficulty, edge cases and refusals included, and no duplicates, PII, or licence problems. More data helps mainly for complex skills or genuinely new domains.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Fine-tuning for behaviour mostly teaches the model a pattern it already has the ability to produce; it surfaces and aligns existing skills. A small set of clean demonstrations is enough to set the pattern. Noise does harm because the model averages what it sees: if half the examples answer in a formal tone and half casually, it will blend or flip unpredictably.

Quality checklist:

  • Correct: wrong answers become learned behaviour.
  • Consistent: one style guide, one schema.
  • Matched to serving: same system prompt, chat template, and tool format.
  • Diverse: cover topics, lengths, difficulty, languages, and typos real users produce.
  • Edge cases: "I don't know", refusals, malformed input, tool errors.
  • Balanced: classes and categories not wildly skewed.
  • Clean: de-duplicated, PII and secrets removed, licences checked.

Practical approach: start with about 200 to 500 careful examples, train, evaluate, inspect the failures, and add data targeted at them. Doubling clean data helps; doubling noisy data mostly adds cost.

sections.label: Code
sections.html: Not applicable: reasoning question; see the split and format questions for code.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Scraping 50,000 examples and skipping inspection.
  • Many near-duplicates inflating one pattern.
  • Mixing several writers' styles.
  • Assuming the "less is more" result applies to teaching new knowledge or skills.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. How do you find bad examples? → Spot-check samples, train a quick model and look at highest-loss examples, and run validators.
  2. When do you need big data? → New language, large new domain, or complex skills.
  3. How do you add data efficiently? → Target categories where eval errors cluster.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3 YOE: "quality over quantity." Senior gives the checklist, starts small, iterates from error analysis, and knows the exceptions.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: Removing 20% of examples flagged as inconsistent labels raised accuracy more than adding 5,000 new ones.

questions.contextHtml: A support-ticket router calls a large hosted model 2.0 million times a day. Each request carries a 1,800-token instruction block with 12 few-shot examples plus about 200 tokens of the ticket. Output is 20 tokens (a category label). Accuracy is 94.1% on a 1,000-ticket labelled test set; p95 latency is 1.6 s. The team has 40,000 historical tickets with human-assigned categories (about 3% estimated label noise). Leadership wants the bill cut by at least 70% without losing more than 1 accuracy point. Assume the large model costs $A per million input tokens and a small model fine-tuned by the provider costs roughly a fraction of that (verify real prices; use symbols or current numbers).
questions.promptHtml: Is fine-tuning the right move, and how do you decide?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Fine-tune, it will be cheaper." No arithmetic, no baseline for a smaller prompted model, no accuracy guard, no consideration of retraining.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: How often do categories change? What is the cost of a misroute? Can latency budgets go lower? What do we pay for tuned-model hosting or surcharge? Are the 40,000 labels trustworthy?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Prompt caching on the static 1,800-token prefix (verify provider support and discount); it may cut cost with zero model change.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) A small prompted model with the same prompt is already near 94%; (b) a small tuned model with a 30-token prompt reaches 94% or more at a fraction of the cost; (c) categories change often so retraining dominates.
  4. How I'd verify each: Run the 1,000-ticket test on the small base model with the full prompt; build a de-noised training set (drop examples where a strong model and the human label disagree, then review them), train on about 5,000 to 10,000 examples, and test on the same 1,000 tickets with confidence intervals.
  5. Root cause: Most of the spend is the repeated 1,800-token prompt on 2.0M calls = 3.6 billion prompt tokens a day.
  6. Fix: If (b) holds, deploy the tuned model with a short prompt: input becomes about 230 tokens instead of 2,000, an 88% cut in input tokens before price-per-token differences. Python sketch of the break-even below.
  7. Prevention: Weekly eval on fresh labelled samples, a category-change runbook with retraining, shadow traffic before cutover, and fallback to the large model when the tuned model's confidence is low.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not tune on all 40,000 noisy labels without cleaning; I would not drop the large-model fallback on day one.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
calls_per_day = 2_000_000
old_in, new_in = 2000, 230               # tokens per call
price_big, price_small = 1.0, 0.25       # relative $/token, placeholders; use real prices
old = calls_per_day * old_in * price_big
new = calls_per_day * new_in * price_small
print(f"saving {(1 - new / old):.0%}")  # ~97% = 88% fewer tokens x a 4x cheaper model (placeholder prices); add training+hosting cost before deciding
val callsPerDay = 2_000_000L
val oldIn = 2000; val newIn = 230
val priceBig = 1.0; val priceSmall = 0.25   // placeholders; use real prices
val old = callsPerDay * oldIn * priceBig
val new = callsPerDay * newIn * priceSmall
println("saving ${"%.0f".format((1 - new / old) * 100)}%")
long callsPerDay = 2_000_000L;
int oldIn = 2000, newIn = 230;
double priceBig = 1.0, priceSmall = 0.25;   // placeholders; use real prices
double oldCost = callsPerDay * oldIn * priceBig;
double newCost = callsPerDay * newIn * priceSmall;
System.out.printf("saving %.0f%%%n", (1 - newCost / oldCost) * 100);

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Tuned model reaches only 92% → Check label noise, add hard examples, or use a router: small model for confident cases, large for the rest.
  • Categories change quarterly → Automate dataset refresh and retraining; if monthly, favour prompting plus caching.
  • The provider deprecates the base model → Keep the dataset and eval so retraining on the new base is a rerun, not a project.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite team cut cost 90% by tuning a small model, then lost the savings in on-call time when category changes arrived monthly without a retraining pipeline.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: says fine-tune with no numbers.
  • Hire: computes token savings, tests small base model, uses the test set to guard accuracy.
  • Strong hire: also tries caching first, cleans labels, adds fallback routing, and plans retraining.

questions.promptHtml: Where does fine-tuning data come from, and what are the risks of each source?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Real projects live or die on data supply. Interviewers want to see practical sourcing instincts.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Five sources: production logs, expert-written demonstrations, synthetic data generated by a stronger model, public datasets, and corrections (user edits and reviewer fixes). Logs match the real distribution but need filtering and anonymising. Experts are accurate but slow and expensive. Synthetic data is cheap and scalable but must be filtered and mixed with real data. Public sets need licence checks. Corrections are the highest value because they target real errors.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Source Strength Risk Mitigation
Production logs Real distribution Contains bad outputs, PII Keep only good outcomes, anonymise
Expert demonstrations High correctness Cost, inconsistency Style guide, review
Synthetic (stronger model) Scale, coverage of rare cases Errors, low diversity, terms of use Validators, judges, execution checks, dedupe
Public datasets Free Licence, domain mismatch, contamination Check licence, sample for quality
User edits / reviewer fixes Targets real mistakes Small volume, biased to what users notice Collect continuously

Synthetic pipeline in plain steps: write seed tasks, ask a stronger model for varied examples, run automatic checks (JSON validity, unit tests for code, rule checks), filter with a judge model, remove near-duplicates, and mix with real examples so the tuned model does not drift toward the generator's quirks.

sections.label: Code
sections.html: Not applicable here; see the dedupe-style checks in the pitfalls and PII scenarios.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Using raw logs including failed conversations as "gold".
  • Generating 20,000 synthetic examples with one prompt, giving 20,000 versions of the same thing.
  • Training on outputs from a provider whose terms forbid it.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. How do you keep synthetic data diverse? → Vary seeds, personas, difficulty, lengths, and dedupe by embedding similarity.
  2. Why are edits so valuable? → Each edit is a paired (bad, good) signal from the real task.
  3. Can logs include customer data? → Only with consent and anonymisation under your policy.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3 YOE lists sources. Senior pairs each with its failure mode, mixes sources, and builds a feedback loop capturing corrections.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A team's synthetic set looked large but near-duplicate; the tuned model overfit to one phrasing and failed on real traffic.

questions.promptHtml: How should you split fine-tuning data into train, validation, and test sets, and what is leakage?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Leakage silently inflates metrics; interviewers want to see you split by group and keep a pristine test set.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: The training set teaches the model, the validation set guides tuning decisions (epochs, learning rate), and the test set is touched only to report the final result. Leakage is when information from the test examples reaches training, so scores look better than reality. Split by group (customer, conversation, document, or near-duplicate cluster), not by random row, so related items stay on one side.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
If 5 tickets from the same customer, written in the same style and mentioning the same account, land in both train and test, the model can score well by recognising the customer rather than learning the task. The same occurs with near-duplicates (a template with a different name) and with the same document chunked into several rows.

Procedure:

  1. Define the group key (customer id, conversation id, source document).
  2. Assign each group to one split, typically 80/10/10.
  3. Dedupe across splits (exact and near-duplicate).
  4. Freeze the test set; do not use it to choose hyperparameters. Use validation for that.
  5. Keep a smaller canary set of general-capability questions to detect forgetting.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
from sklearn.model_selection import GroupShuffleSplit
gss = GroupShuffleSplit(n_splits=1, test_size=0.2, random_state=0)
train_idx, test_idx = next(gss.split(rows, groups=[r["customer_id"] for r in rows]))
assert not {rows[i]["customer_id"] for i in train_idx} & {rows[i]["customer_id"] for i in test_idx}
// Split by group key, then assign whole groups to one side
val groups = rows.groupBy { it.customerId }.keys.shuffled(java.util.Random(0))
val testGroups = groups.take((groups.size * 0.2).toInt()).toSet()
val (test, train) = rows.partition { it.customerId in testGroups }
check(train.none { it.customerId in testGroups })
var groups = new java.util.ArrayList<>(rows.stream().map(Row::customerId).collect(java.util.stream.Collectors.toSet()));
java.util.Collections.shuffle(groups, new java.util.Random(0));
var testGroups = new java.util.HashSet<>(groups.subList(0, (int) (groups.size() * 0.2)));
var test = rows.stream().filter(r -> testGroups.contains(r.customerId())).toList();
var train = rows.stream().filter(r -> !testGroups.contains(r.customerId())).toList();

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Random row split with repeated customers.
  • Using the test set to pick the best checkpoint.
  • Deduping only within train, not across splits.
  • A time-ordered problem split randomly, when it should be split by date.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. When split by time? → When production predicts the future, e.g. test on the latest month.
  2. How do you catch near-duplicates? → Normalised-text hashing, or embedding similarity above a threshold.
  3. What is a canary set? → A small fixed set of general tasks to detect capability loss.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3 YOE: "80/10/10 random." Senior splits by group or time, dedupes across splits, and locks the test set.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A reported 97% accuracy dropped to 81% after regrouping by customer.

questions.contextHtml: You are building a classifier-style assistant that labels customer messages as "complaint", "request", or "feedback". Three contractors labelled 3,000 messages. You compute agreement on a shared 300-message overlap: pairwise agreement is 71%. A tuned model trained on all 3,000 labels reaches only 74% on a held-out set, and it flips answers on near-identical inputs. The guidelines are a one-page doc. A deadline in two weeks makes the PM want to "just add more labelled data."
questions.promptHtml: What would you do?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Label more data." That multiplies inconsistent labels; the model's ceiling is bounded by human agreement.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Are the class definitions ambiguous (is "complaint with a request" one or two)? Is there an expert who owns the answer? What accuracy does the business need?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Freeze further labelling; do not ship a model with 74%.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) guideline ambiguity at class borders, (b) annotator drift, (c) a few annotators systematically off, (d) a genuinely subjective task needing multi-label.
  4. How I'd verify each: Build a confusion matrix between annotator pairs on the 300 overlap; read 50 disagreements; compute chance-corrected agreement (Cohen's kappa) per pair; check each annotator against an expert-labelled 50.
  5. Root cause: Agreement of 71% means roughly 3 in 10 labels are arguable; the model cannot learn a boundary the humans do not share.
  6. Fix: Rewrite guidelines with decision rules and 5 examples per borderline pair, run a calibration round of 100 messages, relabel disagreements via adjudication by an expert, consider adding a "multiple" label, and retrain.
  7. Prevention: Keep an overlap set in every batch, track agreement over time, and audit 5% of samples.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not average labels blindly or train on majority vote without understanding disagreement; I would not hit the deadline by shipping noisy data.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Agreement is still 80% after rewriting → The task may be inherently fuzzy; report calibrated confidence and route low-confidence cases to humans.
  • Budget allows only one more pass → Adjudicate only the disagreement set; it is the highest-value spend.
  • A model-as-judge disagrees with humans → Use it to find suspect labels for review, not as ground truth.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite team added 10,000 labels over four weeks with no gain; a one-day guideline rewrite and 400 relabelled examples did more.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: asks for more data.
  • Hire: measures agreement, fixes guidelines, adjudicates.
  • Strong hire: ties model ceiling to human agreement, sets audits and overlap sets, and defines fallback routing.

questions.contextHtml:
You fine-tune a model to write 150-word product summaries. Training examples have 600-token reference documents plus an answer of about 220 tokens. The training config sets max_seq_len = 512. The tuned model produces good starts but often ends mid-sentence, or never emits its end-of-turn marker and rambles for 400 tokens. Training loss looks healthy at 0.9 and falling. Loader code:

def encode(ex, tok, max_len=512):
    ids = tok.apply_chat_template(ex["messages"], tokenize=True)
    return ids[:max_len]    # silently cuts the tail
questions.promptHtml: What is the bug, how do you confirm it, and how do you fix it?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Lower the learning rate" or "train more epochs"; neither touches the cause.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: What is the token-length distribution of examples? Is the end-of-turn token part of the assistant message? Which framework masks the loss?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Stop serving the tuned model; fall back to the base prompt.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) truncation removes the assistant reply and end token, (b) the loss mask covers a half-cut answer, (c) a template or stop-token mismatch at serving, (d) too-high max generation length.
  4. How I'd verify each: Count examples where len(ids) > 512; decode a few truncated examples and see where they end; check the share of examples whose last token is the end-of-turn token.
  5. Root cause: With 600 prompt tokens, a 512 limit cuts the entire answer. Examples either train on nothing or on a half-sentence with no end token, so the model never learns when to stop.
  6. Fix: Raise max_seq_len above the longest example (or drop or shorten those examples; never cut the answer), and assert at load time.
  7. Prevention: A data validator in CI that fails on any example over the limit or missing the end token.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not truncate from the right silently. Truncating the document side (shorten the context) is acceptable only if the answer stays complete.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
def encode(ex, tok, max_len=1024):
    ids = tok.apply_chat_template(ex["messages"], tokenize=True)
    if len(ids) > max_len:
        raise ValueError(f"example too long: {len(ids)} > {max_len}")  # fail loudly
    return ids
fun checkLength(tokenCount: Int, maxLen: Int = 1024) {
    require(tokenCount <= maxLen) { "example too long: $tokenCount > $maxLen" }
}
static void checkLength(int tokenCount, int maxLen) {
    if (tokenCount > maxLen) throw new IllegalArgumentException("example too long: " + tokenCount + " > " + maxLen);
}

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Only 5% of examples are too long → Still drop or fix them; they teach the model to ignore stopping.
  • Memory prevents a longer window → Shorten the context side, use packing carefully, or use a smaller batch with gradient accumulation.
  • Loss looks fine; why no alarm? → Loss averages over the tokens present; it says nothing about what was cut away.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite job trained for two days on examples whose answers were cut off; a length histogram would have shown it in a minute.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: tweaks hyperparameters.
  • Hire: finds truncation and raises the limit.
  • Strong hire: adds loud validation, checks end tokens, and explains why loss hides the bug.

questions.promptHtml: What is a train/serve template mismatch in fine-tuning, why is it so damaging, and how do you prevent it?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: One of the most common silent quality killers; senior engineers should design to make it impossible.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: The model is trained on text rendered with one layout of special tokens, system prompt, and role markers, then served with a slightly different layout. It never saw that layout, so quality drops quietly: no error is raised. I prevent it by rendering with one shared function (the model's official chat template) for both training and serving, and by testing that the rendered strings are identical.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
A model does not see "messages"; it sees one token stream. A chat template turns roles and messages into that stream, using special tokens such as begin/end-of-turn markers. If training used the template with a system prompt and serving omits it, or an API wrapper adds extra whitespace, newlines, or a different default system message, the inputs are shifted from what weights were adjusted for.

Symptoms: lower format accuracy than the validation set predicted, odd refusals, failure to stop, repeating role markers. Because no exception is thrown, teams blame the data.

Prevention:

  • Use apply_chat_template (or the provider's own fine-tuning API, which handles it) on both sides.
  • A golden test: take 20 example conversations and assert that the training pipeline's string equals the serving pipeline's string, byte for byte.
  • Version the template with the model artefact.
  • Include in training exactly the system prompt production sends (or deliberately none, in both places).
  • For tool use, render tool definitions and results the same way in both places.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
from transformers import AutoTokenizer
tok = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained("your-base-model")  # same tokenizer for train and serve

def render(messages, add_generation_prompt):
    return tok.apply_chat_template(messages, tokenize=False, add_generation_prompt=add_generation_prompt)

train_text = render(msgs_with_answer, add_generation_prompt=False)
serve_text = render(msgs_without_answer, add_generation_prompt=True)
assert train_text.startswith(serve_text)   # serving prompt must be a prefix of the training text
// Kotlin/Java clients usually call a hosted endpoint; keep ONE shared prompt builder
fun buildPrompt(system: String, user: String) = listOf("system" to system, "user" to user)
// Do not re-implement the template in the client; send messages to the server that applies the template.
// Same rule in Java: send structured messages and let the server-side template render them.
static java.util.List<java.util.Map<String,String>> build(String system, String user) {
    return java.util.List.of(java.util.Map.of("role","system","content",system),
                             java.util.Map.of("role","user","content",user));
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Hand-writing the template string in the training script.
  • Different system prompt in production than in the data.
  • Forgetting the generation prompt marker at inference.
  • Changing the base model version without regenerating the data rendering.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. How do you detect a mismatch after the fact? → Compare logged serving prompts with rendered training samples; drop in format accuracy vs offline eval.
  2. Is it an issue with provider fine-tuning APIs? → Smaller risk since they render, but your messages still must mirror production.
  3. What about tool schemas? → Must be serialised identically.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3 YOE knows "use the same prompt". Senior adds the golden byte-for-byte test, version pinning, and ownership of the template in one shared module.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A tuned model scored 96% offline and 78% live; a missing default system message in the serving wrapper was the whole gap.

questions.promptHtml: What is catastrophic forgetting in fine-tuning, and how do you detect and limit it?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: A real cost of tuning that beginners overlook. It tests regression discipline.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: When you train on a narrow dataset, the weights shift toward that task and can erode general abilities such as following other instructions, safety behaviour, or other languages. This is catastrophic forgetting. I detect it with a canary set of general tasks run before and after, and limit it with a lower learning rate, fewer epochs, parameter-efficient methods like LoRA (training small adapter matrices while the base stays frozen), and mixing some general data into training.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Weights are shared across all skills. Gradient updates driven only by "extract invoices" push the weights in directions that help invoices and are blind to everything else, so unrelated skills can degrade. The risk rises with high learning rates, many epochs, and very narrow data.

Detect:

  • A canary eval: 100 to 300 general prompts (instruction following, a few other tasks, refusal checks, languages you support), scored with the same grader before and after.
  • Safety/refusal checks since tuning can weaken guardrails.

Limit:

  • Lower learning rate, 1 to 3 epochs, early stopping on validation.
  • LoRA or similar adapters: base weights unchanged, so you can drop the adapter.
  • Replay: blend 5 to 20% general instruction data.
  • Scope the model: if it only needs invoices, route only invoice calls to it; keep the general model for the rest.

sections.label: Code
sections.html: Not applicable: evaluation process, see the eval-first question for the loop.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Looking only at the target-task metric.
  • Training 10 epochs "to be safe".
  • Assuming a hosted fine-tune cannot weaken refusals.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Does LoRA eliminate forgetting? → Reduces it, does not guarantee it; still run the canary.
  2. How big should the canary be? → Large enough to see a 3 to 5 point drop; a few hundred items.
  3. What if forgetting is unavoidable? → Route by task to separate models.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3 YOE: "the model forgets other stuff." Senior sets a regression budget (for example no more than 2 points on any canary category) and treats it as a ship gate.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A support model tuned on refund conversations began answering unrelated questions in the refund template.

questions.promptHtml: Walk me through how you would evaluate whether a fine-tune actually helped, before deciding to ship.

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: "No eval, no fine-tune." Interviewers want a rigorous, statistically sensible process.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Define metrics and a target, build a held-out test set that mirrors production (including hard and adversarial cases and general probes), baseline the base model with the best prompt and a stronger model, fine-tune, evaluate with the same grader and compare with confidence intervals, check regressions (general ability, safety), measure cost and latency, then decide: ship, iterate, or abandon.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Steps:

  1. Metrics: accuracy or F1 for classification, format validity for structured output, rubric score for open text, plus latency, cost, and safety.
  2. Test set: sampled from real traffic; include rare and adversarial cases; held out from all training. Size matters: with 100 items, a 5-point difference is within noise.
  3. Baselines: base model + best prompt (the thing you want to beat), and a stronger model (the ceiling).
  4. Same grader: if an LLM judge grades, keep the judge model and prompt fixed, and spot-check against human labels.
  5. Confidence intervals: for accuracy p on n items, the standard error is roughly sqrt(p(1-p)/n). With p = 0.90 and n = 400, that is about 0.015, so a 95% interval is around ±3 points. A "2-point gain" on 400 items is not proof.
  6. Regressions: canary set, safety prompts, other tasks.
  7. Operational: latency, throughput, serving cost.
  8. Decision: compare to the target; if the gain does not justify cost, stop.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
import math
def ci95(correct, n):
    p = correct / n
    se = math.sqrt(p * (1 - p) / n)
    return p - 1.96 * se, p + 1.96 * se

print(ci95(360, 400))   # about (0.870, 0.930)
fun ci95(correct: Int, n: Int): Pair<Double, Double> {
    val p = correct.toDouble() / n
    val se = Math.sqrt(p * (1 - p) / n)
    return (p - 1.96 * se) to (p + 1.96 * se)
}
static double[] ci95(int correct, int n) {
    double p = (double) correct / n;
    double se = Math.sqrt(p * (1 - p) / n);
    return new double[]{p - 1.96 * se, p + 1.96 * se};
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Test set built from the training distribution rather than production.
  • Comparing the tuned model with a lazy prompt.
  • Changing the grader between before and after.
  • Declaring victory on a 1-point difference with n = 200.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. How big a test set? → Enough that the interval is narrower than the effect you need to detect; hundreds to thousands.
  2. Paired comparison? → Compare both models on the same items; paired tests are more sensitive.
  3. How do you handle an LLM judge's bias? → Calibrate on human labels, randomise order, and keep it fixed.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3 YOE: "run it on a test set." Senior includes baselines and a ceiling, intervals, regression gates, and an explicit abandon decision.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A 3-point gain on 150 items disappeared in a larger retest.

questions.contextHtml: A tuned contract-clause classifier reported 96.2% on its test set and was shipped. Two weeks later, a customer-success audit of 300 live predictions found 71% agreement with legal reviewers. The dataset was built from 18,000 clauses across 450 customers; the split was a random 90/5/5 by row. Many customers use templated contracts that differ by names and dates. Test performance per customer shows near-perfect scores on the 40 largest customers. Live traffic is dominated by 120 new customers, onboarded after training.
questions.promptHtml: Run the post-incident review: what went wrong and what changes?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "The model overfit; add dropout." It never questions the split or test-set validity.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Was the split by row? Are customers and templates shared across splits? What is the new-customer share of traffic? Was the test set also used to pick checkpoints?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Route low-confidence predictions to human review and inform stakeholders that the 96% figure is invalid.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) leakage via templated near-duplicates across splits, (b) distribution shift to new customers, (c) test set used for model selection, (d) label drift between lawyers.
  4. How I'd verify each: Cluster clauses by normalised text hash or embedding similarity and count test items having a train neighbour above 0.95 similarity; evaluate the old model on the 300 audited items split by "seen customer" vs "new customer"; re-split by customer and retrain as a comparison.
  5. Root cause: A row-level random split put near-identical templated clauses in both train and test, so the test measured memorisation, not generalisation to new customers.
  6. Fix: Rebuild the split by customer (and by template cluster), freeze a test set drawn from recently onboarded customers, retrain, and report the honest number (for example 74 to 80%, to be measured).
  7. Prevention: Group-aware split utility in the pipeline, near-duplicate check across splits as a CI gate, a rolling live-audit sample, and an offline-vs-online gap alert (here 25 points).
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not just collect more data from the same customers; that deepens the leak. I would not blame model size.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Time-based split gives 68% → That is the honest estimate for new customers; improve with more diverse customers and templates.
  • Legal reviewers disagree 10% with each other → That caps achievable agreement; measure against adjudicated labels.
  • Customers refuse data sharing → Evaluate per-customer holdout and use few-shot adaptation per customer.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite team found that deleting one template cluster dropped test accuracy 12 points; the metric had been rewarding recognition of boilerplate.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: blames overfitting without checking the split.
  • Hire: identifies row-level leakage and re-splits by group.
  • Strong hire: quantifies near-duplicates, audits live data, adds CI gates and an offline-online gap alert.

questions.contextHtml: A fine-tuned model checks whether an uploaded expense receipt is compliant ("yes" or "no" plus a one-line reason). The training set has 12,000 examples, 91% "yes" because logs came from approved expenses. Offline accuracy on a random held-out slice is 93%. In production, finance finds the model approves 97% of receipts, including 38 of 40 deliberately non-compliant test receipts (95% false approvals). Reasons given are generic ("Receipt appears to meet policy"). Training loss was low and smooth. A teammate suggests the prompt needs more instructions.
questions.promptHtml: Diagnose and fix.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Add prompt instructions." This ignores the dataset skew and the misleading accuracy metric.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: What is the class split in train and test? Where did the "no" examples come from? Do the reasons carry real content? What is the cost of a false approval vs a false rejection?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Disable auto-approve and route everything above a spend threshold to human review.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) class imbalance: predicting "yes" always yields 91% (near the 93% score); (b) the sample was approved-only, so "no" examples are rare and unrepresentative; (c) reasons are templated shortcuts; (d) a prompt problem.
  4. How I'd verify each: Compute a majority-class baseline (always "yes" = 91%) and compare; report recall for "no" and the confusion matrix; read 50 reasons; test on a balanced adversarial set.
  5. Root cause: The model learned the shortcut "answer yes", which gets 91% on skewed data. Accuracy hid it because the metric rewarded the majority class.
  6. Fix: Collect or synthesise genuine non-compliant examples (reviewer rejections, rule-based generation, then verified), rebalance to roughly 50/50 or weight classes, require specific reasons referencing receipt fields, evaluate with recall and precision on "no", and retrain.
  7. Prevention: Report per-class metrics; keep a balanced adversarial test set; compare against the majority-class baseline in every eval report.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not oversample the same 100 "no" examples hundreds of times (overfitting). I would not rely on accuracy alone.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• True compliance rate in production is 92% → Evaluate on a balanced set for recall but calibrate thresholds on the production prior.
  • Few real rejections exist → Mine auditor corrections and generate rule-violating variants, verified by a rule engine.
  • Reasons still generic → Add a structured output (cited field values) and validate it against the receipt.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite approval model scored 94% by never rejecting; a one-line "always yes" baseline in the report would have caught it before launch.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: tweaks the prompt.
  • Hire: spots imbalance, computes the majority baseline, adds negatives.
  • Strong hire: uses per-class metrics, adversarial test set, specific-reason validation, and cost-aware thresholds.

questions.subtopic: PII and secrets in training data
questions.contextHtml: A support assistant was tuned on 25,000 anonymised-by-regex chat logs. A week after launch, a user prompts "my order email is" and the model completes with a real-looking customer email and phone number; the security team confirms it appears in the training data in a form the regex missed (email written as "name at domain dot com"). A red-team probe extracts 14 distinct personal strings from 2,000 attempts. The privacy lead asks whether you can "remove that person's data from the model."
questions.promptHtml: How do you respond and what do you change?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Add a system prompt saying don't reveal personal data." The data is in the weights; prompting does not remove it.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Which data categories are present (contact details, payment, health)? What are our legal obligations and deletion deadlines? Is the model exposed externally? Which dataset version trained it?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Take the model out of service or put an output PII filter in front while retraining; open a privacy incident with the privacy lead.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) regex missed obfuscated formats, (b) names or addresses were never targeted, (c) duplicated examples encouraged memorisation, (d) metadata leaked via free-text agent notes.
  4. How I'd verify each: Run a stronger PII detector (NER-based plus regex plus an LLM review) over the dataset and compare with what the regex caught; extraction probes using prefixes from training examples; count duplicated records.
  5. Root cause: Incomplete anonymisation plus repetition let the model memorise rare personal strings, and nothing tested for extraction before launch.
  6. Fix: Rebuild the dataset with layered PII removal (detectors, then sampling audit), dedupe, remove the affected person's records, retrain from the clean data, and run extraction tests before release. Answer the privacy lead honestly: deleting from weights is not reliable, so retraining without the data is the real remedy.
  7. Prevention: PII scanning as a pipeline gate, data minimisation (drop fields not needed), extraction red-team in the release checklist, retention rules for training sets, and model/dataset lineage records.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not claim the output filter "fixes" the model; it is a stopgap. I would not keep the old model online while waiting.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Retraining takes two weeks → Keep the model offline or behind strong filters and a base prompted model as fallback.
  • Regulators ask for proof of deletion → Provide dataset lineage, the retraining record, and extraction test results.
  • Could differential privacy help? → It limits memorisation but costs quality and effort; consider for sensitive domains, verify feasibility.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite team found a customer's phone number came back after a prefix prompt copied from the training data; the scrub had only covered the standard formats.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: relies on a system prompt.
  • Hire: removes the model or filters, rebuilds the data with better scrubbing, retrains.
  • Strong hire: adds extraction tests, lineage and retention, and is honest about unlearning limits.

questions.subtopic: Synthetic data and terms of use
questions.contextHtml: A startup has only 400 real expert-written examples for a legal-drafting assistant and plans to generate 40,000 synthetic examples with a frontier hosted model, then tune an open-weight 8B model. A first run on 40,000 synthetic examples gives 82% on the 150-item expert test, versus 85% for the frontier model with a prompt. Reading the sample, the synthetic examples share the same opening sentence in 35% of cases, and 6% contain wrong citations. The legal team asks whether the provider's terms allow training a competing model on its outputs.
questions.promptHtml: Do you proceed, and how would you improve the plan?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "More synthetic data will close the gap." This ignores diversity collapse, errors in the generated data, and the terms-of-use question.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: What do the provider's current terms say (read them; get legal sign-off)? Is there a second permitted teacher? What are the quality, cost, and latency targets? What does "competing" mean for this business?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Pause training on outputs until legal clears the terms; continue with data from permitted sources.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) low diversity (35% share a template opening); (b) factual errors (6% wrong citations) are learned; (c) too little real data in the mix; (d) the 8B student has a capability ceiling.
  4. How I'd verify each: Measure diversity (n-gram overlap, embedding clusters), check citations with an automated validator against a legal database, train with 400 real + 2,000 filtered synthetic vs 40,000 raw, and compare on the 150 items (with intervals; 150 items is small, so expand to 300).
  5. Root cause: Quantity was substituted for quality; the generator prompt lacked variety, and no filter removed errors.
  6. Fix: Diversify seeds (clause types, jurisdictions, difficulty, personas), validate citations programmatically, drop near-duplicates, judge-filter, keep all 400 real examples at higher weight, and consider an open-weight or permitted teacher.
  7. Prevention: Data cards recording source, teacher model, and licence terms; automated quality gates; periodic human audit of 100 sampled examples.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not ship a model whose training data may violate a licence. I would not accept 82% vs 85% as a win until the interval is narrower and the cost saving is quantified.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Filtering leaves only 3,000 examples → Fine; test whether 3,000 filtered beat 40,000 raw; usually yes for behaviour.
  • The student beats the teacher on the test set → Suspect leakage or a test set that mirrors the generator's style; verify against real expert-written cases.
  • Citations remain wrong → Use retrieval or a lookup tool at inference; do not expect an 8B model to memorise law.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite team's synthetic set had one favourite phrase in a third of examples; the tuned model started most answers with it, even where it made no sense.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: scales synthetic generation without checks.
  • Hire: filters for diversity and errors, mixes real data, flags terms of use.
  • Strong hire: gets legal sign-off first, validates citations programmatically, tests filtered vs raw sizes with proper intervals, and moves facts to retrieval.
